claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Cooling-rate variation and isothermal holds provide a controlled comparison against rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching from the high-temperature state will retain predominantly single-phase BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Al diffuses more slowly than Co, Fe, and Ni under the relevant cooling and exposure conditions.
Differential atomic diffusivity during cooling drives local compositional partitioning.
During moderate or slow cooling and isothermal holds, Co, Fe, and Ni redistribute more rapidly than Al.
Diffusivity-driven redistribution produces regions with altered local composition.
The resulting local compositional changes destabilize the initial BCC lattice.
Local partitioning promotes heterogeneous nucleation and growth of additional phases.
Moderate or slow cooling and prolonged isothermal exposure provide sufficient atomic mobility for phase evolution.
Rapid quenching or very-low-temperature holds freeze the composition before significant partitioning occurs.
Changing the cooling history can change the observed microstructure and phase assemblage.
Slower cooling and/or isothermal holds will produce secondary phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 relative to rapid quenching.
The secondary phases may include FCC, intermetallic, or other structures.
The identities and proportions of secondary phases depend on transformation kinetics and local composition.
The cited prior evidence supports the proposed role of differential diffusivity.
A lack of significant local partitioning after slow cooling and isothermal holding would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Nucleation of any secondary phase in a rapidly quenched sample would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction says rapidly quenched samples will 'largely' retain BCC and the baseline is only 'predominantly' single-phase BCC, both of which allow a minor secondary-phase fraction. The falsification rule instead treats nucleation of any secondary phase in a quenched sample as decisive falsification.
